Wide receiver DeAndre Moore on the Go-Go offense: “It allows players to have freedom – go get open”

From CUBuffs.com … Ask DeAndre Moore Jr. how he would explain Colorado’s offense to a friend, and the Buffaloes wide receiver does not reach for a diagram.

“Backyard football,” Moore said.

That is the shorthand. The longer version, the one Moore gave a few seconds later, gets at why the Colorado Buffaloes football team believes its offense can look different this fall.

“I see this offense as an offense that allows the players to have freedom,” Moore said. “We have a lot of options to do whatever we want to do, and it’s not just, oh, you have to run certain routes to beat the coverage. No, bro — go get open. He allows that freedom, from the tight end room to the running back room to the receiver room. It’s a whole bunch of flexibility.”

The “he” is offensive coordinator Brennan Marion, whose Go-Go system has been the central project of camp’s opening week in Colorado Springs. Marion said the install takes time, largely because the offense is built to bend toward whoever is running it.

“It takes time to install it, from the standpoint of just all the things that it’s capable of doing,” Marion said. “It’s really an engine that’s run off of players. So based off what we have, based off what we can do with our players, we adapt it to that. There have been a lot of pages in the book. There have been pages stolen from other people’s books, so there are a lot of things that we can pull out and look at because of the skill set of players that we have.”

For the players, the adjustment has been less about memorizing and more about reacting.

“To piggyback on what he said, just from the running back perspective, it’s a lot more — you get to play reactive,” running back DeKalon Taylor said. “It’s not necessarily like you have to stick to a scheme. It’s whatever you see, go for it, because whatever you see, it’s probably right. So I really enjoy it. It kind of takes me back to being like a little kid almost.”

Taylor, a speed back, has been described from the outside as a tailor-made fit for the system. He does not disagree. He also does not think the description belongs to him alone.

“I’m pretty excited for what I can do, but not even just me,” Taylor said. “We have so many weapons in the room. We’ve got so many weapons from the receiver room. The O-line is amazing. Overall, anybody in this offense can go at any given time.”

The freedom comes with a cost, and Marion has been direct about it. Playing multiple spots in multiple formations asks more of skill players than many of them were asked at previous stops.

“From the standpoint of the skill position guys, they have a lot on their plate, from the standpoint of multiple formations, multiple guys getting the ball,” Marion said. “Some of our guys came from places where one guy just dominated the ball. You line up on the left side, run a go route, OK — until you play a better team, and then you don’t have any catches because you don’t know motion, you don’t know how to be on another side. You don’t know how to play multiple spots. Where our guys play basketball on grass, musical chairs. They move to multiple spots.”

What does not move is the run game. Marion called the ability to run the football a staple of what the offense does, and he wants the group that does it to look like a defense while it does.

“You have to be physical and violent,” Marion said. “We practice offense with a defensive mentality. We love contact. We love physicality. We relish in that. But as far as the physicality and the violence, if you were able to see practice today, you would see a lot of bodies hitting the ground. It was very violent in the trenches.”

CU media restrictions on open practice information: A complete blackout

Press release to media attending open practice

From CUBuffs.com …

OBSERVATION ONLY
This practice is open for viewing purposes only. It is closed for all reporting, recording and documentation purposes. Nothing observed at practice may be reported, published, posted, broadcast or otherwise shared in any form, on any platform, at any time.
NO DEVICES
Cell phones, tablets, cameras, video equipment, audio recorders, meta/smart glasses and any other recording-capable devices are prohibited. Devices will be bagged and stored and returned upon leaving.  This applies to all attendees, including credentialed media.  This is where the backpack will come into play.  If you just leave your phones and all other devices in your backpack upon arrival, we will have them back to you when we get to room 319.  If you are only coming to practice and not the media availability, you will have to put your phones in the bag upon arrival with the rest of the public attendees.  It’s likely best to just leave them in your car at that point.
NO DOCUMENTATION
No note-taking of any kind — written, typed, dictated or otherwise. No photography, videography, audio recording, sketching or diagramming. No live coverage, live posting or real-time updates of any kind.
NO REPORTING
The following may not be reported or characterized in any way, during or after practice. This list is illustrative, not exhaustive:
  • Injuries, player participation status, limited or modified participation, or the presence of any player in a non-contact jersey
  • Depth chart, rotations, personnel groupings or position changes
  • Offensive or defensive schemes, formations, alignments, play calls, signals or terminology
  • Trick plays, special teams looks or situational packages
  • Individual player performance in team or competitive periods
  • Any tactical, strategic or personnel information of any kind
If you are uncertain whether something is reportable, the answer is that it is not. When in doubt, contact the Athletic Communications Office before publishing anything connected to this practice.
ENFORCEMENT
Violations of these guidelines may result in removal from the facility, revocation of credentials and restriction of future access for the individual and the outlet, consistent with CU Athletics media policies.

AT&T announced as CU’s official wireless sponsor 

Press release from CUBuffs.com … AT&T, one of the most recognized brands in the world, is now the official wireless/wireline sponsor of University of Colorado Athletics through an agreement secured by CU Athletics’ exclusive multimedia partner, Learfield’s Buffalo Sports Properties, the CU Athletic Department announced today.

The sponsorship, which is tailored to fit the current dynamic environment of college athletics, includes exclusive branding on the Dragon Seats climate-controlled sideline benches that are used on the home and visiting sidelines, digital branding through athletic facilities, and support of student-athlete NIL initiatives.

“We are so thrilled to have a legendary brand like AT&T join our Buffs family,” said Director of Athletics Fernando Lovo. “This sponsorship is the perfect fit for CU Athletics in that it helps support our student-athletes and their Name, Image, and Likeness dreams while also featuring AT&T throughout our facilities, including Folsom Field.”

“CU Athletics represents one of the most dedicated fan communities in collegiate sports,” said Amanda Cacheris, VPGM Southwest, AT&T. “Through our communications partnership with CU Athletics, we are proud to support Colorado’s rich traditions, deepen fan engagement, and invest in the vibrant community that powers the Buffs.”

AT&T was also the presenting sponsor for Black & Gold Weekend on April 10-12, which featured a variety of community events including youth football and flag football games, a Colorado High School Coaches Summit, and the annual Black & Gold intrasquad scrimmage. After the game, over 4,000 fans were invited onto the field to get autographs and photos with their favorite Buffs players.

“We’re excited to help bring this collaboration to life between AT&T and Colorado Athletics,” said Andrew Popchock, General Manager of Buffalo Sports Properties. “By aligning AT&T with high-impact branding and meaningful fan touchpoints, this program will deliver value across the entire Buffs community.”

Buffalo Sports Properties, the locally based team of Learfield – the leading media and technology company powering college sports – is the exclusive multimedia rights holder for Colorado Athletics and oversees all sponsorship agreements on behalf of the Buffaloes.

Could this be the year CU returns to a physical, fundamentally sound defense? 

From BuffStampede.com … As the first week of CU camp gets close to the end and the Buffs get ready to head back to Boulder, we are starting to get a clearer picture of what Chris Marve wants to do with his defense. Violence, aggression, physicality, and relentless effort may not be what you want to see from your kids on the playground, but it is exactly what you want to see from a Big 12 defense, and that is what Marve has been preaching and pushing all week. One thing is sure: Marve knows how to fire his guys up, and his speeches to both the team and to his defense have that kind of old-time gospel preacher vibe to them that make you want to get up and find Jesus—and run through a wall to do it!

But fire and brimstone aren’t the only tools that Chris Marve has at his disposal. He is a coach who knows a lot about defensive football, and as a career LB coach, he knows a thing or two about the front seven on defense. And with all the different fronts seen in modern football, and the adjustments on those fronts—bear, over, under, tite, mint, and more—sometimes the best answer is still something basic and old school, like a straight-up 4-3 defense.

It doesn’t require a doctorate in space engineering to figure this out—when you have three really good linebackers, you find ways to keep all three of them on the field, particularly against run-first offenses.

There has been a lot to like in this first week on defense for CU, not the least of which is that the rest of the defense seems to have taken up edge rusher Immanuel Ezeogu’s winter mantra as the basis for their play (“I didn’t come here to f*** around”). It has been a minute since CU fans consistently saw truly relentless effort and physical, violent, fundamentally sound play on defense. Could this be the year it happens?

*Everything Coach Prime had to say at his Fall Camp press conference*

Opening comments

“I’ve been through here (Colorado Springs) and been here to visit donors and all of that stuff, but this is my first time really spending time here. It’s been an absolute blessing meeting the mayor and a couple of his counterparts, the superintendent, as well as yesterday going to the Air Force. That blew my darn mind. First of all, how beautiful it is… It is unbelievable. They were wonderful. The coaching staff welcomed us with open arms. They talked about the intricate details of attending Air Force and what they must go through to get in.

“Our kids talked about our disciplines, and they talked about their disciplines, and we ain’t like them. They are unbelievable. The way they have the basic training is unbelievable. I’m thankful that we had the opportunity to go do that. I’m thankful that the city has opened its arms, and the campus that we’re staying on, it’s great.”

On wide receivers coach Jason Phillips’ retirement

“He really coached last year for me because I was going through what I was going through, and he didn’t want to leave me in that situation, so we had already talked about it. Rashad (Davis) has been with us since Jackson State. I don’t think you guys know that. Rashad has been with us for quite some time, and sometimes people may give credit to others. J-Phil did a great job, but Rashad has been there since Jackson State, doing a phenomenal job. He’s done a lot of legwork. He’s done a lot with the receivers. He’s been there, so it was his time to rise up, and we’re thankful and happy that we have him.”

On Danny Scudero’s injury

“Danny’s progressing. We got some good news the other day. We’re optimistic. We’re hoping he’s going to return sooner than later. He’s probably, most definitely, is going to play against Georgia Tech for sure. But I know Danny; he’s definitely gonna do that. Other than that, we’re wonderful.”

Reason for opening camp in Colorado Springs

“We wanted to go somewhere away that was significant, not just around the corner like 45 minutes, 30 minutes. We wanted to get away so they couldn’t have the contacts to drive back home on an urge. Even though we’re on buses, they’re not doing that. No visitations or anything like that. No outside food coming in. They’re doing a great job of feeding us. They’re off the phones. We monitor that, and they’re really getting to know each other and really getting to bond. I sat at the table with a group of guys yesterday, and they was telling stories about some of them were sleepwalking and walked out of the room. And one of the coaches also fell out the bed, and he got a bruise on his arm.

“It’s been some wonderful stories that has transpired on the campus. Also, when we come face to face with the deer, so we love it. We’re bonding. We’re getting closer. We’re getting to know each other.”

Growth from the spring until now

“Unity, togetherness, them really understanding one another, understanding what the coaches desire, getting a feel for tempo in the way we practice. Practices have been wonderful, very competitive. You see skirmishes and see fights; you’re gonna see that. If you don’t see that, something’s wrong. If you’re having contact with you for the first time in quite a while and you’re trying to win a position, win a job, and you don’t have that passion, that fire in you when somebody goes across the line, something’s wrong. So we’ve had that. I’m not applauding that by any means, but I’m happy. I’m pleased with the effort that we’re giving.”

Why this new group is different

“This is not to demean any of the former coaches, but this is the best staff I feel like I’ve ever had in my coaching career, from youth all the way up. These guys are good, fundamentally sound, creative, innovative. They’re born leaders. They’re head coaches that are coaching the offense and defense. The young men are responding to them. Even special teams, we’re doing that in a conglomerate effort. We’re unified on that. The defense is teaching these two special teams, offense has these others. It’s been great. I love the energy that these coaches are providing, and a new group of kids helps out tremendously.”

Applying pressure

“I apply pressure. I don’t feel pressure. You know what pressure is? That’s a single momma trying to make ends meet. There ain’t no man in the house, and she got to be the mother, the father, the provider, the disciplinarian and everything. There’s a person lying up in the hospital right now with cancer, that they had some bad news that they may have a multitude of weeks to live. That’s pressure. This is football. I’m really good at this. I can play this. I can coach this. I can do this. If you don’t believe, you don’t believe. God bless you. I need that. I like that. You’re putting me in my comfort zone there. I’d rather be booed than clapped or applauded, because if you start clapping too much, I’m not gonna trust you.”

Moving forward

“We have a whole new team, we have a whole new staff, and you’re still talking about last year? We don’t think like that. I could try my best to sit here and turn my neck all the way around and it won’t go back. I’m right here, man. I’m right here, and I love the young men. I love the coaches. We even have a new AD.”

Injury updates on Kam Perry, Taj White

“Kam will be alright. Kam will be straight.”

On White: “Everybody’s gonna be good.”

Offensive line observations

“Physicality. When you rotate guys, you bring them through like that. When you’re able to have eight to nine guys that can really start for you, you’ve got to find a way to get reps. You got to find a way to show love and show them appreciation and respect and understand that you got a room (where) now one guy goes down in practice, it’s next man up. But you have the depth that you could do that. These guys ain’t no joke, man. They are violent.

“When we recruited, we recruited mentality. It wasn’t just size and stature and status of where they came from. It was a mentality that they displayed on the field. It was a mentality that we spoke about when they came in to be recruited with their mothers and some with their fathers and loved ones. It was the mentality I was looking for in the conversations that we had, and all of those young men, they have that mentality. Even some of the ones that we held over, because anybody that didn’t have it, we got rid of them.”

On patience

“Much more at certain levels, at certain positions. I’m not patient with the secondary by any means, because that’s my thing. Probably with the receivers as well, because that was my thing as well. I’m a little more lenient on other positions that I probably wasn’t as involved in. But to have the patience and not understand and not think that I’m going to get from this guy what I got from that guy years ago, you can’t think like that. You’ve got to develop a certain thought process and mentality.”

On roster turnover

“I don’t think we’re the only ones with a new group of people… I was just one of the first ones to do it. When you’re the first one to win the race, everybody’s not applauding, they’re not clapping because they’ve never seen that before. But now, once everyone else is doing the same darn thing, remember when we first got here? You guys made a big deal out of the portal. Now everyone’s doing it. I don’t see you attacking them the same way you attacked our program in regards to the portal. If you do the homework on it, which we’ve done, I think we’re right there with many other schools in the turnover that’s forecasted.

“I wish you could understand the mentality and the heart of Boo Carter from when he came, from where he is. I wish you could understand some of these young men that are playing on this team right now, from being closed off and just having the windows up to now showing love and expressing love and allowing because they trust the coaches that they have their best interests at heart. But it’s a revolving door in college football because of the portal. You drop it down to one year, I’m pretty sure one school that you could change to or transfer to, I’m pretty sure you get a different type of roster for everyone else.

“But if you truly got out there and did your homework, you would understand we’re right there with many other schools in the transferring numbers. We don’t wish to have that multitude of transfers every year, but you got to really do your homework and think about the year, what you’re paying, what their productivity is.”

Potentially practicing with Air Force

“That’s something I’ve been suggesting for quite some time, haven’t I? And the NCAA felt compelled to allow FCS schools to do what we thought of quite some time ago. So we’re not involved. They won’t allow that, but even if we could just practice at the same location, it would do it justice. We don’t have to compete against one another. But I wish one day we could have a spring game against one another. It’d be wonderful for the state, it’d be wonderful for both cities if we did home and away. It would be a great look for college football and Colorado football.”

On Gideon Lampron

“He comes to practice every day. He’s smart, intelligent, a born leader, physical, mean. He gets upset when he don’t make the play. He lives this, he loves this. He’s a football player. He’s that guy that when you watch his tape, when you watch him on film… Getting to know him, he’s one of the best dudes on the team. He gets along with everybody, and I’m pleased.”

Renewed energy

“I’ve learned how to really live life and love the life I live, and live the life I love. I’ve learned how to take up more time for myself and for my family. I’ve developed another level of understanding of how good God is. Last year at this time, I wasn’t as able, and I wasn’t as strong and as vibrant and as ready as I am right now. I’m thankful for everything I’ve gone through. It’s been a tremendous journey, but it’s going to be a good one. The script that’s being written right now is going to be unbelievable. I cannot wait to look at some of you and just smile.”

–

August 5th

… CU in a few minutes … 

OC Brennan Marion: “I know how to do receiver in my sleep. Give me any guys, and we’ll find a 1,000-yard receiver out of him”

Assessing the running back room – All of those guys can be explosive. Been very violent, running downhill. They’ve done a better job in protections. That was the challenge from the spring to the summer, to understand protection. Those guys have been doing a really good job of understanding the protection and then being physical at the point of attack and protection. So the number one rule if you want to play in the National Football League at running back is you have to protect the quarterback. So, coach (Johnnie) Mack and coach (Joc Upton) have done a really good job of helping those guys understand protections and working with the offensive line to get it done. So, really proud of that group from a standpoint of trying to be three down backs, being able to catch the ball out of the backfield, being able to run the ball. They’re all here because they can run the ball when they get the ball, and then being able to protect the quarterback, obviously being the most important thing.

On how relationship with JuJu Lewis has developed – I think anytime you have the type of ability that that kid has coming out of high school, and all the people that try to get around a kid who’s supposed to be the next coming that creates trust issues. So for him it’s just about the consistency of him seeing me be me every day, and it’s giving him more confidence to be himself and open up to the group, and just let his personality really thrive and show. So he’s continuing to grow every day, he’s still a young kid. He still has a lot of growth to do. He’s not going to be a final product year one or sorry, year one and a half, or however we look at that. But he’s doing a really good job of being the same guy, consistent every day, and his teammates are respecting him for that.

Reaction to people calling CU small – One, I have zero reaction. And the other one I have is, as the kids would say, pull up. So we’re small, we’re this, we’re that, whatever. I mean, at some point you got to spot the ball and see. So that’s my mindset on it.

Learning each time he installs the Go-Go offense with a team – Yeah. When I first learned the West Coast offense when I was in junior college, it was explained to me like it’s a language. So at the time, there was 32 NFL teams, and there was probably like 20 to 24 running the West Coast system. So if you were a player and you got traded on a waiver wire or whatever, or you got cut, you could go to another team and you would know the terminology, the verbiage. So over the years, being with guys that have called plays in the NFL, guys who have played called plays in college, guys who have called plays in high school, seeing all the different terminology, putting it together, making it mine. And then the form unique formations that we use. Now, when I say it to the guys, it’s kind of like a language. It’s kind of foolproof. So now you see multiple teams using it – NFL, college, high school. Everybody’s kind of adapting some of the plays because the verbiage and the terminology is really easy to communicate.

August 4th

… CU in a few minutes … 

DC Chris Marve: “We track everything, so we have objective data that says, ‘Either you’re getting it done or you aren’t’ “

Defensive coordinator Chris Marve is seeing some improvement in CU’s defense.

“Certainly growth between practice one and practice two,” said Marve on Tuesday. “I think they’re communicating really well, they’re playing together. We preach a lot about violence and aggression, relentless effort. I think that’s been pretty visible. I think the pads come on tomorrow, so now we get to play some real football.”

Marve said the Buffs need to get pads on before he can truly evaluate how the defense has improved. However, improvement has been evident.

“What I will say is that I have noticed a significant amount of information retention because of how we’ve taught it and how we’ve been very succinct in our language and very clear in how we communicate it,” he said. “And how we allowed the access for the players to us, but also the information. So, certainly, I’ve seen some fruits of it so far.”

Because there are so many new players – and coaches – starting roles and playing time roles are up for grabs. Colorado football opens the season Sept. 3 at Georgia Tech.

“We track everything,” Marve said. “We track your one-on-one percentage in pass rush or in pod work, your win or loss rate. We track your win-loss rate versus player A, versus player B, versus player C. We track your effort to the ball. … We track your production.

“We track everything, so we have objective data that says, ‘Hey, either you’re getting it done or you aren’t.’ Then we show it and we teach in a way and we lead in a way to try to get behaviors replicated. If those behaviors are rewarded, hopefully it permeates the defense and everybody’s thinking and doing the same thing.”

–
